newsitem.title: SPAIN: Explosion in suspected ETA hideout in Spain.
newsitem.headline: Explosion in suspected ETA hideout in Spain.

text.p: An explosion in an apartment led to the discovery of an ETA guerrilla hideout packed with weapons on Thursday, just days after a killing by Basque separatist rebels that sparked national outrage.
Police investigating the blast in the Basque town of Durango said rebels living there had accumulated a powerful arsenal and were preparing to carry out a series of bombings and grenade attacks.
Authorities were searching for at least three suspects who fled the hideout after a grenade apparently went off by accident, officials said.

The Basque regional government said investigators found no connection between the residents of the rebel "safe house" and the killing last weekend of a politician, 29-year-old Miguel Angel Blanco, which ignited massive anti-ETA demonstrations across Spain.
Spanish state radio reported, however, that at least two of the Durango fugitives had been under scrutiny for possible links to the murder.
Gestoras Pro Amnistia, an ETA prisoners' rights group allied with the radical separatist movement, said one man was arrested, but the claim could not be officially confirmed.

With Spain still seething with anger over Blanco's killing last weekend, scores of police descended on the small town after a loud explosion ripped through a fourth-floor apartment. No one was injured in the blast.
Authorities reported finding 16 grenades and nine launchers ready for firing along with bomb parts, detonators and chemicals.
Police blanketed the area and set up roadblocks.
The massive police response reflected the sense of unease that has pervaded the Basque country of northern Spain since Blanco's murder.

Millions of people have taken to the streets throughout Spain to vent their outrage. In some cases, angry crowds have clashed with ETA sympathisers. Authorities have expressed fears that the rebels may retaliate by escalating their attacks.
In the Basque city of San Sebastian, officials have been bracing for a demonstration planned for Saturday by ETA's political wing, Herri Batasuna.
The Basque regional government on Wednesday barred ETA supporters from going ahead with the protest for fear that it would ignite more violence.
Herri Batasuna said on Thursday it had filed an appeal in a local court and would call off the weekend protest if the government ban was upheld. A ruling was expected on Friday.
"There's no demonstration on Saturday unless the judge says that it is legal," Herri Batasuna leader Floren Aoiz told reporters.
Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar and other Spanish politicians have branded Herri Batasuna "accomplices" to murder and have sought to isolate it.

In Strasbourg, the European Parliament banned a former Euro-deputy, Karmelo Landa, who is a leading member of Herri Batasuna. Landa, a deputy until 1994, will be denied access to all of the parliament's buildings in Brussels, Strasbourg and Luxembourg.
"We cannot allow him to use the European Parliament to make apologies for terrorism," said Jaume Duch, the parliament's presidential spokesman.

Blanco was kidnapped last Thursday by rebels demanding the transfer of 500 ETA inmates to prisons in the autonomous Basque region within 48 hours. The government refused and ETA shot him twice in the head on Saturday. He died 12 hours later.
ETA has killed nearly 800 people in its 29-year struggle for an independent homeland.
But it was the death sentence carried out against an ordinary low-level functionary that cut to the heart of Spanish society and sparked an unprecedented public outcry.
